items.en: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence.

Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.
Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days.

“From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.”

The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.”

Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said.
Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much.
“I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter.
Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million.

Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app.
Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists.

The kidneys, which are similar in size to human ones, were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.
The results are a big milestone. But the team still needs to establish whether the approach could work for humans.
How much more can nuclear power plants give?

In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about the nuclear industry trying to do just that.

Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. On October 5, the Department of Energy awarded Vistra a $4.2 billion loan to upgrade three plants.
Pushing existing reactors to produce more could quickly provide more clean power for data centers. But just how much additional power can we count on?

Joan DiFuria and Stephen Goldbart started treating the neuroses of the newly rich during the dot-com boom in the late ’90s. “All these young people were coming to us with questions about meaning and purpose and fear that had to do with the impact of sudden money in their lives,” says Goldbart. Other mental-health professionals had dismissed these clients’ problems — they were rich, so how bad could things be? — but Goldbart and DiFuria believed they were experiencing something unique: a condition they would eventually call “sudden wealth syndrome.”

Goldbart, a psychologist, and DiFuria, a therapist, co-founded the Money, Meaning & Choices Institute in California in 1999. Together, they’ve worked with hundreds of individuals and families who’ve come into more money than most people can possibly imagine, typically through company equity, IPOs, or inheritance. But now, as wealth disparity reaches dizzying new heights in the U.S., their clientele has become even more disoriented. “It’s sudden wealth syndrome 2.0,” says DiFuria. “All these people coming out of the AI boom are experiencing wealth on a different level, and having more complex emotions about it, too.” Namely, these recently minted one-percenters seem to be more depressed, isolated, and paranoid about their money than Goldbart and DiFuria have ever seen before. Here, the two share how sudden wealth syndrome is manifesting today, the misguided ways that some people deal with it, and how they try to steer the world’s richest people out of their bubbles.
You popularized the concept of sudden wealth syndrome decades ago. How would you define the symptoms now?

Stephen Goldbart: We coined the phrase to capture the cluster of symptoms and issues associated with new or sudden money in people’s lives, ranging from existential anxiety to narcissism to severe identity disruption to depression. That’s when we began to use the term “sudden wealth syndrome” and to build an understanding of it and a set of programs to help folks deal with it.

Joan DiFuria: One of our goals with clients is to help them find their comfort zone with wealth. We had a lot of clients come in and talk about their sudden wealth at age 28, 35, 37. Other therapists would say, “Well, what’s the problem? You’ve got money, you don’t have to worry.” But they also had a lot of anxiety, guilt, embarrassment, shame, even hubris. And they would say, “I don’t know, do I keep working? Do I stop working? I’m too young not to work, but I don’t know if I should work.” So we’d start asking them questions about values and purpose and meaning, and that was really helpful to them.
What are your respective backgrounds? How did you develop this specialty?

SG: I’m a clinical psychologist by training, and I also have a background in organizational development and business consulting. I don’t come from wealth, but I’ve always been comfortable around business and financial matters, and I’ve always been interested in how human beings navigate major life transitions.

JD: I had an extensive international business background working in the copper industry. Then, I did a career transition and became a licensed therapist. I worked with high-level CEOs at places like Charles Schwab and Salesforce. A lot of therapists are intimidated by high-profile people with a lot of money, but I found it fascinating. Their money might put us in different worlds, but I’m there to focus on the soul of the person, to help them through something they couldn’t talk to anybody about. The billionaires we work with want to admit the difficulties they face and some of the guilt and shame they feel, but there’s not a lot of people they can talk to.

Yeah, it’s hard to feel bad for a billionaire. But it’s also not the worst thing for them to question their wealth, right? I can’t imagine that anyone believes this level of disparity is good for society.

SG: Exactly. But it also creates a scarcity mentality and culture of narcissism: “It’s all about me. It’s dangerous out there. I need to protect myself and I need to build protection from risk.” That culture is much bigger today than it was 20 years ago, there’s no question. It creates social isolation. People who have derived wealth from AI, they very much have their own subculture. It has a dark side, this sense that this money can result in something very negative for society.

JD: We’re hearing news every day about how destructive AI can be. So if you’re already feeling anxious about your wealth and the whole world is saying, “What you’re doing is going to kill me or take my job,” how do you speak to your friends? How do you speak to your family? That sense of guilt and embarrassment and shame is exacerbated a thousand times. It’s really next level from what we’ve seen before.
You mentioned hubris earlier. I’m curious how you respond to people who believe they’ve become so rich because they’re special or chosen in some way.

JD: They’ll say, “I’ve earned it. I worked hard.” And I say, “Well, people who work three jobs have worked hard and earned their money, too, and they’ll never make what you make.” But most people with narcissism are not going to come to ask us questions about values or purpose.

SG: Our clients are self-selecting. And it’s more common for a young new wealth holder to look at this impact and ask, “How does this fit with the rest of my life? Are people going to like me for me or for my money? What are my friends going to think? How are they going to relate to me or connect with me?” So the younger you are and the less experienced you are in life, the more likely this is going to have an impact on you. And it can be devastating.

JD: We had one recent client, a young guy. He was responsible. He made money. He was secure. Then, boom. He invested in AI and he became one of those big-time winners. Suddenly he feels anxious, upset, embarrassed, guilty. He doesn’t know what to say to his friends. He hides out. He feels very alone. He feels he cannot date women because how would he relate to them? He said, “My world fell apart. I wish this had never happened to me.” And we hear that a lot.
Well, that begs the question: If money is making these people so unhappy, why don’t they just give it away? Do you ever see clients who do that?

SG: If you’re looking at a 28-year-old who’s worked for Anthropic for three years and has no background in money, it takes them a while to think about what they want to do with their lives. If you’re young, and you’ve recently come into sudden wealth, you don’t know what your plan is yet. And for a lot of these people, that initial honeymoon phase is fun. It’s a high. And it takes a little while to come down from it into having a more articulated and nuanced plan of action.

They need to do some strategic life planning. And part of that, we hope and encourage, is giving back. As our clients mature through stages of wealth-identity development, most of them do find that they want to give back significant amounts of money, and we help them. Usually, they’re very interested in doing it, but first they need to get clear on what they want for themselves, for their family, and for the wider world.

It seems like there’s a lot of fear around giving money away. And I understand that people are afraid they might need the money for a health emergency or some other disaster, for example. But how do you encourage clients to push past that fear when they really do have way more than they could ever need?

JD: The question becomes, how much is enough? The reality is that most of our clients first want to take care of themselves. Then they want to take care of their children and their families. And then they want to give back. With some families, it’s all for their kids. But now they’re starting to see that all that money can have a detrimental effect on their children’s self-esteem, motivation, and sense of agency. There’s drugs, alcohol, suicide, and they don’t want that. So they’re asking, “What do we do to give them enough, but not so much that they end up depressed?”
Then you have people who are afraid to give their money up at all. Usually, there’s some psychological issue going on, like a hoarder mind-set — they just can’t let it go because they’re afraid.

Conversely, we’ve had very young people come to us and say, “Look, this money is dirty. I want to get rid of it.” And we go, “Okay, you can do that, but you’re only 25. What happens if you get sick? Look at an equation where you’ve taken care of yourself, then give the rest away.”

Then, of course, some of our clients are just buying more homes. One of our billionaire families at first felt guilty about doing too much spending. But now they’re into yachts and planes, and they moved to an area with a lot of other billionaires like them. During our last meeting, they said, “We found our people. We don’t have to be embarrassed or hide the fact that we have a plane and a yacht and five homes. We can finally be open about it.” So we’re seeing these new gated communities developing around these billionaires, where they can be out and proud and ready to roll.
Wow. I’m curious how you feel about that.

JD: Well, the short answer is that if I’m going to help a family, and I care about these people, I have to be Switzerland. I can’t let my judgments or my feelings interfere with the integrity of my work. But it is hard with so much suffering in the world today, and with disparity getting bigger and bigger. We thought the wealth gap was big in the 1990s, when we first identified “sudden wealth syndrome” and started doing this work. But the disparity is so much bigger now. And it’s really, really hard to come to terms with it.

Let’s say I was a 32-year-old early employee at Nvidia, and I came to you and said, “I’m suddenly a centimillionaire, and I come from a humble background and my whole family feels like they can’t relate to me, and I’m not even sure if I believe in what our company is doing anymore.” What would you have me do?

SG: We’d sit down with that individual and get them to say out loud all their questions and concerns about spending, saving, sharing and transferring their wealth, and help normalize their experience. Then we’d help them craft a set of operational values that will drive their financial and lifestyle decision-making. You’re not a wholly different person, but you have a set of resources that your family and friends don’t have, and that’s real. We’re creating a safe and neutral space for them to explore this stuff. Our whole approach is grounded in the idea that there’s a learning curve, and it’s going to be lifelong. We help them separate the money from who they are as a person. The money’s a fraction of who you are; it’s not all of who you are. We don’t want to confuse the fraction with the whole.

JD: We also set a concrete plan with deliverables. What are you going to do? When are you going to do it? With who? If they say one of their values is “I want to give back to the community with my time and resources,” then we move it into action. How much time do you want to spend on that? Are you going to volunteer on Fridays and give X amount to certain organizations? It’s often a very long initial meeting we have with these clients: around six hours.
What else makes today’s billionaires different from the ones you’ve worked with in the past?

JD: The level of security. For example, we just got a new client referral. Normally, we look up the names of people who are referred to us, but lately what’s happening is that nothing is available. We can’t find out anything about this family. They’re so rich that they have security companies come in to scrub their internet presence every single day.
So it’s like they can afford to disappear.
SG: They’re buying whole enclaves, maybe in Lake Tahoe or the Hawaiian islands. We’re talking about large amounts of real estate, not just a nice home. They’re building a bubble for themselves.

JD: There are compounds where each member of the whole family can have their own home and their own pools, and they have managers to do everything from cleaning your rugs to getting you hangers to licking your stamps. They can do whatever they want and buy whatever they want. They take private jets between their many homes around the world. And as a fantasy, all of those things sound great. But the reality is that it’s a lot to take care of. They’re spending so much time managing their managers, and it feels imbalanced to them.
If you’re so rich that you can afford to cut yourself off from the rest of the world, it doesn’t seem healthy for the individual. But it’s also not beneficial to society at large.

SG: No, it’s not. It’s a major social problem, really. To be fair, many of the tech wealth holders we’ve worked with have been extremely philanthropic. But from a more sociological standpoint, is our society drifting toward a great imbalance between the haves and have-nots, with the rich people up on the hill, cut off from everybody else below them? I think so. And is that a good thing? Well, of course not. Because, ultimately, we’re all in it together.

JD: Most of us go where we’re comfortable. We find friends we can relate to. But what’s happening now is that extreme wealth is on a different level. People are raising children who have barely ever left the house. They don’t know what a poor person looks like. And it’s so comfortable to live in these gated communities of billionaires that they become more isolated and lose all connection to the real world. Do they have any idea what society is really dealing with?
How do you manage people like that, who are so entrenched in their bubbles?

JD: Well, a lot of them probably wouldn’t seek us out. But we also have the luxury of assessing our clients before we take them. We wouldn’t want to work with a narcissist. Some people believe that because they made the money they have, they’re smarter than someone else, and that’s their psychological defense. We want to work with people who are concerned about the welfare of their next generation and the community around them, people who feel that their wealth brings a sense of responsibility.

Whalefall is a movie that primarily takes place in the heaving guts of a sperm whale. Before getting into the how and the why of the stomach-centric predicament its hero finds himself in, it’s worth noting a few things about the movie’s pedigree. It’s based on the 2023 novel of the same name by Daniel Kraus, who this year won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for Angel Down, about American soldiers in World War I who discover an angel who’s been shot down over a battlefield in France. Kraus has a foot in the realm of film, having written books with Guillermo del Toro and completed George A. Romero’s unfinished manuscript for the 2020 novel The Living Dead, and he co-wrote the script for Whalefall with its director, Brian Duffield. Duffield got his start as a writer himself, though in 2023 he got attention for directing No One Will Save You, an alien-invasion movie starring Kaitlyn Dever that managed to drum up acclaim even after having been sent straight to streaming. This is a movie with more on its mind than just a high-concept premise, is what I’m saying, though the outrageousness of that premise really can’t be ignored. A goddamned whale swallows a guy whole! He gets trapped in its belly!

By my count, it takes around half an hour for Whalefall to get to tummy time. Until that point, it’s a straightforward family drama about grief and regret that features some striking imagery, especially when it comes to depicting the velvety deep. Abrams, here for more torment after spending Resident Evil on the run from infected mutants and impending fatherhood, plays Jay Gardiner, the youngest of three siblings, and the only boy of the family. Unlike his sisters, Eva (Jane Levy) and Nan (Emily Rudd), Jay had a strained relationship with their father, Mitt (Josh Brolin), a grizzled sea dog who got along better with the local Monterey scuba-diving community than he did his own son. Mitt, who’d been struggling with mesothelioma, took his own life a year earlier, strapping on a weight belt and going over the side of a boat into the ocean he loved so much. Jay fled to landlocked Iowa for college and has only come back to California for the anniversary of Mitt’s death. Possessed by a determination he can’t really explain, he sets out alone one early morning with his old dive gear, intent on recovering his father’s still-lost remains. Out there among the kelp beds on the edge of the Monterey Submarine Canyon, he runs instead into a sperm whale that’s ventured out of the deep in pursuit of a giant squid.

When an errant tentacle catches his ankle, Jay gets pulled into the whale’s maw along with the squid and wakes in the tough-walled first chamber of its stomach with enough oxygen to last him an hour. Whalefall is a movie about trying to get out from inside a whale doing its best to digest you, and also a heartfelt movie about grief, and it can never quite get these two aspects to entwine, though it tries, mightily. I’m not entirely onboard the Abrams train yet, but he reliably holds the screen alone in the claustrophobic interiors of the whale, where the organic walls are always threatening to close in. As Jay tries to avoid getting crushed by the whale’s stomach in one quivering chamber or dissolved by acid in the next, Abrams comes up with reactions that feel as plausible as possible in a situation that’s totally unimaginable. He’s better at being funny than he is at suffering — a bit in which Jay carries on an emotional one-sided conversation with a bioluminescent jellyfish is a high point — but when he needs to project agony, he brings it, and he brings it while shrieking in pain or laughing in delirium around a diving regulator.

It sounds silly to say this movie about getting swallowed alive is gnarlier than you’d expect, but at times Whalefall veers into body horror in its contemplations not just of what it means to become food, but to be inside a creature far more suited to the hostilities of the sea than we are, and able to dive to depths we were never meant to see. Less successful are the ways in which Duffield cuts between these near-death experiences and flashbacks to Jay’s relationship with Mitt, who was relentlessly hard on the son he wanted to raise in his image while punishing him for his perceived inadequacies. Brolin can play a compulsive hard-ass like Mitt in his sleep and is thoroughly believable as a blue-collar guy who can’t help but push around his kid in the name of love, who talks at Jay about nature and then taunts the boy for his lack of interest in his dad’s view of the world. But in condensing their relationship to these interludes, Whalefall turns their father-son strife into something archetypal and sometimes hackneyed — Mitt bellowing “Soft lungs!” at Jay when Jay jumps off their boat to get away from him plays more like a laugh line than a moment of permanent rift.

Still, there’s something to the earnestness with which the movie does finally have its daddy issues and its cetacean ones intersect. It happens in a sequence of haunting imagery and hallucinatory conversation that’s admirable, even if it doesn’t work. Plenty of movies are About Trauma these days, but it’s rare to see one that’s willing to be so literal about the connection. Whalefall goes all the way, unapologetically turning the idea of a young man being encased in his father’s toxic masculinity into text — and into a potential tomb of whale flesh he has to try to escape.

In May, I sat in a living room on the fringes of Hangzhou, one of the most technologically advanced cities in China and home to Alibaba, Unitree, and DeepSeek. In many ways, the party that was about to start resembled one that you’d find in any coastal metropolis: ten professionals in their 20s padding barefoot across the carpet, snacks on the dining table. Only the laptops scattered across the floor and couch suggested this was a different type of social gathering, one that has grown common in the past three years in China’s towns and cities. Our host, KC, has gathered a small circle of friends to learn AI.

KC’s face is still marked with acne; he is tall and thin, barely past 20, and already a vibe coder of some local fame. Today he’ll teach others how to use Codex and Figma to quickly build websites, Electron desktop apps, install packages — but the first step is teaching everyone to “put up the ladder,” the euphemism for deploying VPNs and relays that bypass OpenAI’s geo-block. Like any self-organized class, it doesn’t really begin until nearly two hours in. Only as the sky darkens do people settle down, grow patient, and start the class.

The demographic of the room is young, hungry, yet refusing to join or be excluded from the rat race of big tech — they self-identify as engineers, designers, influencers, or, to use a more fashionable term, one-person companies (OPCs). They are members of a social species typical of a generation facing 18.9 percent unemployment, astronomical real-estate prices in big cities, and a battered post-COVID economy, which a friend describes as petit bourgeois, overeducated, downwardly mobile young people who can just barely make the rent. A few years ago, low-cost towns like Liangzhu (where KC lives), Dali, and Anji started actively courting digital nomads and vibe coders like them. Amid government campaigns and a stream of social-media posts, young people started washing up there, hoping that learning AI while keeping their expenses low might change something.

During the self-introduction session, one woman mentions, a little shyly, her old life at Tencent — which she had disliked so much that she quit to explore “the many ways of not going to work.” Another, with long black hair, introduces herself as a novelist serializing a long book on Jinjiang Literature City, China’s biggest women-focused web-fiction platform. A third says she used to work in fashion and now runs an “aesthetics and shopping-companion” business with a friend and does self-media and AI projects on the side. They are all convinced that AI could empower their work.

Since ChatGPT, a new consensus has hardened across China’s tech industry: AI is the next mobile internet. On the surface, the country seems to have arrived at a near-universal embrace of new technology. Xi Jinping has described AI as an essential engine for China’s “new quality productive forces.” From a Marxist-Hegelian perspective, AI is on the right side of history, and history must march forward. As Evan Osnos, a staff writer with The New Yorker, recently wrote, the future could be made in China. But beneath the AI frenzy lies a real dread: people’s fear of being thrown overboard by China’s next Darwinian round of industrial upgrading, with little choice but to go along.

At once an old Chinese reflex returned: When history accelerates and people lose their bearings, find a teacher. In a society where meritocracy and education still carry near-religious authority, the proper response to a disruptive technology is to embrace it and to enroll. Decades ago, it was “English fever,” when English-learning-as-self-transformation swept factory floors and university lecture halls alike, everyone convinced that fluency was their ticket out. Now the conviction has simply changed languages. Resisting this technology is futile, unwise — so better to seize the window before it closes. The state claimed AI will empower thousands of industries, with social-media timelines filled with proof that someone, somewhere, has already changed their lives with it. In response, for many people I met across China since the arrival of ChatGPT, one thing that kept surfacing was their hunger for learning about AI, a compulsion to keep upskilling. Lessons, lessons, lessons — I noticed how often the word surfaced during casual conversations.

In the U.S., backlash against data centers has united people across the political spectrum and generations. This “AI populism,” a term coined by the writer Jasmine Sun, reflects a belief that AI is not a neutral technology but an elite project driven by tech billionaires to concentrate power and displace workers. In China, on the other hand, a meme that’s now circulating goes: Westerners get restless when they can’t protest; Chinese people get restless when they haven’t found a teacher. People like KC self-organize classes; for others, the dread of getting left behind by AI has presented a business opportunity.

Hangzhou’s Future Sci-Tech City (未来科技城) is one of those municipal declarations of intent to materialize the future. It is home to Alibaba’s headquarters and to the towers, campuses, incubators, talent apartments, and financial-service complexes through which a local government announces that it, too, belongs to the next technological epoch. For the sheer density of engineers packed into its office parks, people jokingly call the area “the center of the programmer universe.”

The industry of paid knowledge, and its priesthood of “knowledge influencers,” is nothing new — in the mobile internet age, people built an entire economy around it. Now this industry has a new direction: evangelize AI. The company I’d come to see was the operator of one of the largest “make money with AI” communities, a membership business that monetizes the promise of AI. The company is called Shengcai Youshu (生财有术), roughly “The Art of Getting Rich.” It offers online classes, offline intensive training, and co-working space. Its Hangzhou office, where the founders sit, is one of the larger nodes in a network that spans the country. I was greeted by Mr. Tree, a middle-aged AI influencer on the company’s payroll, whose bio announces him to the world as being on a mission to “look for 100 business answers in the age of AI.” He is habitually nervous, easily and overly excited. His accent is not the polished, elite-educated kind, and he mispronounces his English words.

In one of the short videos of him teaching a class to a few dozen, he stands onstage before an audience old and young, their faces solemn, pens moving. “What is AI?” Mr. Tree asks loudly. “AI is your Silicon-based labor force! Most companies run nine-to-five, eight hours a day. AI runs 7-by-24 — round the clock, every day of the week!” Mr. Tree’s relentless high spirits are contagious, and they remind me of a Mormon elder in Orange County who once tried to bring me into his church when I was a college student freshly arrived from China. He walked me through the office, recording the whole tour on his DJI Osmo Pocket, as though everything he did needed to become material for his vlog.

The office’s theme color is green, the color of money (in fact, the company offers a class called “Making Dollars Together”). Meeting rooms have names like “Apostle of the Method” (传术师) and “Evangelist” (布道师). Along the corridors, the walls are covered, like those of any company proud of its own legend, with founder lore, milestones, and mottos. I read that the founder, Yiren, after leaving Alibaba in 2017, vowed to “help young people who, like him, had once been poor but hardworking, change their fate by making money,” the kind of declaration you might hear from a gilded-age robber baron or a self-made oracle like Benjamin Franklin or Jack Ma — mission fused seamlessly with the libertarian lore of self-salvation. Another line on the wall managed the same mix of sincerity and self-regarding heroism: Whatever saved you, use it to save the world.

That afternoon, when I visited the office, Yiren happened to be in. We shook hands politely. He was thin and shy, soft-spoken, his hair combed with a precision bordering on severity. It was hard to square this quiet figure with his career: a man with a cult following who had recently turned himself into an AI chatbot (on WeChat) and issued a standing invitation: Ask me anything about growth, entrepreneurship, your projects, or making money.

Yiren first found influence online writing paywalled dispatches with titles like “365 Ways to Make Money in a Year.” As paid followers grew, his company, The Art of Getting Rich, funneled that traffic into something far more elaborate. Today, paid members are encouraged to collect something called Dragon Balls — a goofy, gamified name for the points awarded to those who help the community grow: posting useful content, recruiting newcomers, and then climbing the leaderboard. On one wall, a diagram lays out the order of ascent. You begin as an ordinary member by paying the yearly fee, then become a Dragon Ball holder, then a Navigator, then you enter the Deep-Sea Circle — the executive tier — until, at last, you gain access to the co-working floor among the senior members and stand, in effect, at partner level.The higher you climb, the more people and resources become available to you. Am I in a cult? I wondered. The headquarters of some pyramid scheme?

Membership is not cheap. Entry to the online community costs ¥3,365 today, against an average Hangzhou private-sector salary of ¥7,671 a month, roughly half a month’s wages for an ordinary worker. What keeps people coming, I think, is a residual faith in upward mobility — the hope that behind a changed economy there remains a way in. The company is now nine years old, with more than 80,000 paying members to date and over 2,000 offline events hosted per year across Chinese cities. The more I read the company website — which promises to help people “break into new circles, trade notes with bosses and operators, find a community that fits, and never walk the road to wealth alone” — the more it resembled a kind of church, a place where career, marriage, and a child’s education might all be worked out.

Mr. Tree took me into a room with 20-odd people in their 20s to 40s. Some were solo entrepreneurs and senior members using the office as a co-working space, heads down at work. Mr. Tree asked everyone to stop so he could introduce me as a visitor from San Francisco, prompting someone to shout, “Take us to Silicon Valley!” The whole office laughed.

Beyond The Art of Getting Rich, which hosts AI courses of every kind, the cheaper, messier imitators — “DeepSeek 101,” “Get Wealthy With AI,” “Learn to Distill,” “Super AI Agent” classes — have now multiplied to fill every corner of the internet. AI is the only path forward. The last chance for ordinary people to defy fate and remake their lot. AI won’t replace people, but people who can’t use AI will be replaced by people who can. Before the pitch, the sellers usually offer a few tidy success stories: a stay-at-home mother, for example, who used DeepSeek to turn out video scripts at 30 yuan a job. Since last year, state-sponsored media has taken to calling this paid-knowledge economy a mess, warning that ordinary people are being “cut like leeks” — fleeced — by a course-selling economy that “takes advantage of people’s ‘skill anxiety’ about new technologies.” Online, I found one member’s verdict on The Art of Getting Rich’s own classes:

“Tried The Art of Getting Rich for a few days. Pricey! Over a thousand yuan. Got inside and found nothing of substance: they have the students themselves post their money-making stories to fill the place up, and if you post enough you can offset the tuition.”

And yet. After the office visit, I read some of the articles shared on the company’s news feed, and to my surprise, they were not bad. One walked through pairing Claude with Obsidian to create a kind of product-copy engine, for the struggling e-commerce seller managing a sprawl of listings that each needs its own picture-and-text blurb. This article explained “the attention that AI tends to dilute,” and how to manage “context window,” and the way to prevent models from suffering “pattern collapse” and turning lazy. Most of it didn’t strike me as novice knowledge; Claude and Obsidian are no strangers to Silicon Valley’s hyperproductive tech set. But picture the reader who might actually pay ¥3,365 to learn it further. Maybe he’s a man in his 40s with a middle-school education, somewhere in China’s export-dependent manufacturing belt, running his business on instinct and hard work but not a word of English. He sells water bottles, desk lamps, and plastic toys across the border to the richer half of the world and is in a perpetual battle with the blank spot where the Amazon product copy should go. Picture him handed Claude and Obsidian. The distance the article is trying to close is enormous, and it is closing it in earnest.

These are the people Mr. Tree and The Art of Getting Rich mean to reach: the ones from traditional manufacturing, from trades with no exposure to AI at all. In June, he posted, to his own feed, a thank-you note from one of his students, another typical profile:

“I’m working as a security guard right now. I came across The Art of Getting Rich late last year … for more than half a year I’ve been using all kinds of AI without stop … every day at work I’m interacting with Claude Code, on my phone and on my computer at home. My stint as a guard is almost over now — I’m about to start a job at a semiconductor-packaging company! Once the new work settles, I’ll keep building my AI skills.”
Mr. Tree’s caption reads: “Dude says he’s a security guard. Hell of a thing.”

This spring, a Chinese sociologist named Lian Si published A Journey Without a Map, an ethnography of ten groups of young people. Si is no dissident. He is executive vice-president of the China Youth University of Political Studies. Yet even from inside the system, his verdict lands hard. Many young people in their 20s are living in a reality unlike that of previous generations who could take economic miracles for granted. Uncertainty has become an ordinary fact of daily life, with risk seeping into every part of life — school, work, home, and marriage. I thought, Even a Party-approved scholar is allowed to say that now. His counsel to the young: Stop climbing. “Make peace with the ordinary,” he has said. “Shake hands with failure.”

In my search for a story about China’s AI optimism, I instead found stories about choicelessness and coping — about a crippled sense of agency, narrowed down to the few things still within reach, in a world that offers only one correct way to make sense of your own struggle: It would be your own fault if you got left out. Here is a state with vanishingly little upward mobility, promising “common prosperity” anyway by doubling down on high technology. When the Party holds fast to a Hegelian History — History with a capital H — in which technological ascent is not a choice but a necessity, what options remain?

If Mr. Tree’s story is true, then this silver lining is real — the upward mobility AI promises isn’t something people simply conjured out of desperation. Xiaokai, a 25-year-old film director I met near Hangzhou, is an example.

If you didn’t already know that he employed seven people and ran an AI video studio turning over several million yuan a year, his manner and thick Dongbei accent might place him as a street-corner hustler. Every 30 minutes he gets up to smoke. He wears slippers and a pair of beige shorts, his long hair tied back at the nape. Xiaokai’s humor is the Dongbei kind: bleak and wearily cynical, interspersed with random self-deprecating commentary, no tolerance of pretense or bullshit.

Xiaokai left his home in Dongbei, China’s rust belt, at 18 to chase a dream of acting. Like many children of the Dongbei, he grew up while his parents were away as migrant workers. His was a lonely childhood, and he was raised by a grandfather and a television playing Jackie Chan and old Shaw Brothers films. Before he discovered Way to AGI (one of the largest AI-learning communities online) in 2023 and taught himself AI filmmaking, Xiaokai thought he was a man with no prospects: a third-tier diploma from art school and behind him a string of failed ventures, livestreaming among them. Dongbei people make the best livestreamers, he told me. When he opens his mouth, the street smarts pour out, and you understand at once that this is a man who will never let himself go hungry.

Beside Xiaokai sat Big Wang, 42, Xiaokai’s COO. He’d been up all night working on a video for a district government in Shanghai, a celebratory piece, all gleaming towers and grand accomplishments, in the house style you can call the old cadres love. The peculiar challenge of this government commission is that the AI video needs to convincingly resemble a real production, complete with drone footage and a big-budget feel. Every building, every detail has to be faithful to the real thing — which is why Big Wang had spent the night hunting down each hallucinated tower and street, until nothing in the frame was something the machine had dreamed up. The trick, Xiaokai explained, is to conduct a whole orchestra of AIGC models into setting still images in motion — the right prompts, endless small adjustments — until a three-minute city documentary leaps onto the screen, sweeping and grand, the camera gliding as though it had really been there. Shot conventionally, he said, the thing would cost well over a million yuan. This one went for around a hundred thousand. At lunch, he insisted on paying and ordered far more than we could eat.

Neither of them could have pictured the life they have now — so much work coming in that they are up through the night without rest. The company does so well that they can’t say aloud what a single commission costs, for fear of the envy it would stir among their peers. They showed me a screenshot of one rival’s message, sent in pure spite. “He saw how much we’re pulling in, saw we’d landed a big one,” Xiaokai said, “and he just lost it.” Xiaokai’s social media is a model template of Chinese Gen-Z success, a timeline crowded with highlights: red carpets at the Beijing and Shanghai film festivals; his work aired on CCTV, the state broadcaster; the press anointing him “the first Gen-Z in China to turn AIGC into money”; and, flaunted for all to see, the 2024 Award of Excellence in the AIGC Short-Film section of the Beijing International Film Festival.

With today’s AI capabilities, Xiaokai explained, the best kind of plot is “a story that keeps losing people”: As it advances, it sheds characters, so you have to worry less about consistency. (Too many faces is a real problem in the current state of the models — the longer the clip, the more the features begin to warp and slide.) A perfect project, then, would be an Agatha Christie–type story — characters are trapped in isolated settings, then disappear one by one. Then he showed me a clip: a knife pressing slowly into human skin. The sound raised goosebumps over my whole body. “Look — the blood coming out, how real it looks. Killer.” He pointed it out to me, delighted with himself.

Even as a success story, Xiaokai is emblematic of a market so grim it demands endless grind. (I visited Xiaokai’s studio on a Saturday; three people were still working and all looked sleep deprived. They only take one day off each week.) Next year he plans to put a down payment on an apartment and get married — at a moment when the overwhelming majority of 20-somethings like him are adrift in China’s simmering deflation and cruel job market. He joked that once he had checked off the to-do list of his life, he’d finally make art about his hometown.

Dongbei is in deep demographic decay. Its young people leave for school and rarely return. A genre has emerged under the name “Dongbei Renaissance,” composed of films, fiction, music, all circling the region’s postindustrial ruin and its bleak iconography: abandoned factory compounds, laid-off workers, family shame, murder, violence. The people who make them are the children of the 1990s state-enterprise collapse looking back on their parents’ wrecked world, a point of view that has carried a constellation of writers and filmmakers into the mainstream.

Xiaokai wants to turn his core memory of Dongbei into an AI film. The memory, as he described it: a wide frozen river beside a vast, emptied factory town. Every winter the river froze thick enough to walk on. To keep from slipping, people scattered coal cinders across the ice; the coarse grains bit under a boot or a tire and held.

Xiaokai described every detail as though the film already existed. It’s a story about a father and a son. Across the frozen river runs a thin black path — coal ash the father has laid down, stroke by careful stroke, so that the son, away in some distant southern city, can find his way home safely. But the father dies before the son returns. The son learns of the death, comes home, and finds the ice long since melted.

In Silicon Valley, the running argument between the accelerationists and the doomers is premised on the idea that AI is the only variable that matters. It could go extraordinarily well or extraordinarily badly; utopia or dystopia will arrive in a matter of years, even months. The great AI researchers assured me, all the same, that one day we will stand to superintelligence as apes stand to us. But when I think of the film Xiaokai wants to make, or read the latest gospel Mr. Tree posts, or catch up on KC’s new projects, what stays with me is not Silicon Valley’s arithmetic about AI or Beijing’s grand plan, but people’s stubborn insistence on their own dignity, defiant of a future the big men are summoning.

An estimated 22 million Americans currently use cannabis as a form of sleep aid, and almost one in four says they're likely to try the drug to help them sleep.
But despite the widespread view that cannabis can help you get a good night's rest, the evidence is starting to suggest otherwise.

In recent years, scientists have linked cannabis to sleep disruption, and reviews have suggested that the drug may in fact have an overall detrimental effect on sleep quality, despite what many users might think it's doing for them.
A new study in JAMA Network Open highlights this paradox, suggesting a possible disconnect between the sleep quality of cannabis users and their own perception of how well they're sleeping.

In an analysis of 35 years of observational data from participants in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, researchers found that cannabis use was associated with multiple objective measures of poorer sleep.
Subjectively speaking, however, based on questionnaires in which participants rated their sleep quality, there was no sign that people using the drug felt their sleep was negatively affected.
"This study challenges the common belief that cannabis helps people sleep better," says epidemiologist Thanh-Huyen T. Vu from Northwestern University.
"Our findings suggest cannabis may actually be associated with poorer sleep quality, even if people don't perceive those changes."

The CARDIA study began recruiting participants in 1985 from four sites across the US, ultimately involving over 5,000 people. Participants completed several follow-up examinations as the study progressed, with the ninth follow-up assessment taking place in 2022 (year 35 of the study).

In the new analysis by Vu's team, the researchers looked at data from 1,266 participants in the CARDIA cohort, including 1,128 people who self-reported sleep assessments at the end of the study period.

They also analyzed objective sleep data from 891 participants who used a wrist-worn tracker to monitor their sleep for seven days, with 753 people contributing to both the subjective and objective analyses.

After adjusting for age, race, sex, education level, smoking and alcohol use, and other factors, the researchers found that greater lifetime cannabis use was associated with a lower sleep percentage (the amount of time asleep during sleep periods), higher sleep fragmentation, and waking up for longer periods during sleep.

Each additional year of cannabis use was linked with poorer sleep, equating to 10 percent higher odds of a low sleep percentage (spending less than 85 percent of the sleep period asleep), 4 percent higher odds of high sleep fragmentation, and 21 percent higher odds of prolonged waking up (spending at least 30 minutes awake in total during sleep periods).

Among recent cannabis users (participants who had consumed the drug within the last 30 days), cannabis use was linked with longer sleep duration (20 minutes extra per night), but also with lower sleep percentage, higher sleep fragmentation, and longer periods of waking up, compared to people who had never used the drug.

Yet despite all these objective measurements indicating poorer sleep, neither lifetime nor recent cannabis use was associated with the participants reporting lower subjective sleep quality, the researchers note.
"This was one of the most interesting findings," says Vu.
"The wearable device detected more nighttime disruption among participants with long-term cannabis exposure, but the participants themselves generally did not report worse sleep."

While we can't be entirely sure why this is happening, the researchers say the discrepancy could have important public health implications, especially given cannabis's popularity and reputation for being a supposed sleep aid.
"Individuals may not perceive declines in sleep quality or may interpret longer sleep duration as improved sleep despite objectively poorer sleep," the researchers write in their paper.
"Thus, cannabis-related sleep disturbances may go unrecognized."

The researchers note that previous studies examining cannabis's effects on sleep quality have shown mixed results, but they observe that many studies have been limited by small samples, short follow-up periods, or cross-sectional designs that didn't examine how long-term cannabis use is associated with sleep quality, and few studies have incorporated objective sleep data.
Further, some studies examining the effects of medical cannabis may have only looked at sleep as a secondary outcome, or may have assessed it alongside other factors that may affect sleep.

"One possible explanation for the small improvement in subjective sleep quality observed in these medical cannabis studies is that most participants were from clinical populations with pain, cancer, or sleep disorders," the researchers write.
"Cannabis may improve perceived sleep quality by reducing symptoms that interfere with sleep, even when objective sleep measures show little or no change."
Given this was an observational study, the research can't establish whether cannabis use directly caused the sleep disturbances people experienced.

The researchers also acknowledge a number of limitations, including that they didn't track cannabis potency or timing relative to sleep, and while their study did incorporate objective sleep measurements, they were only able to access a week's worth of sleep tracking data (over a study period lasting decades).
They suggest future long-term studies with objective sleep assessments will be able to better clarify how cannabis use influences sleep.
In the meantime, if you really want to aid your sleep, the research team says following the conventional advice is probably a smarter choice than consuming cannabis.

"Keep a regular bedtime, make your bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and avoid looking at phones and other screens right before bed," says neurologist and study co-author Kristen L. Knutson from Northwestern University.
"It can also help to establish a calming routine before sleep, such as reading, meditating or taking a shower."
The findings are reported in JAMA Network Open.

The Army has long been dependent on space capabilities to navigate terrain, communicate in hard-to-reach areas, and identify and strike targets. Now, the service wants to deepen its space operations expertise and is making plans to expand its own cadre of operators in the coming years.
In June, the service established its a Space Operations Branch, consolidating space-related career paths and created to train Soldiers to operate and deploy space systems.

This week, during the annual Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting in Washington, after transverring 600 enlisted Soldiers into the branch Oct. 1, Army officials predicted the Space Operations Branch will eventually include thousands of officers and troops.

The 600 transfers were reclassified as 40D Tactical Space Operations Specialists, the Army’s Military Occupational Specialty code for space troops—uniting them with 40A Space Operations Officers. The enlisted Soldiers had previously been temporarily reassigned to space-related units from Air Defense Artillery, Signal, and Military Intelligence fields.

Speaking with reporters Oct. 14 during the conference, Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, director of the Army’s Transformation Integration Directorate for Space Superiority and High Altitude, said the service’s space operations cadre has almost doubled since 2012, and he expects that to continue within the new Space Operations Branch.

“When we talk about the branch and the targets, having a couple thousand dedicated folks within the branch, between the enlisted and the officer side, is a significant contribution across the service,” Mroszczyk said when asked if the Army has a target level of growth for the branch. He didn’t offer more specifics on how long it might take the service to get there.

After the Space Force was created in 2019, space operators and units transferred from the Air Force, Navy, and Army, with the bulk of Space Force operators coming from the Air Force. Army officials have continued to make the case that they need to have their own space-focused Soldiers. While critics charge that this risks duplicating effort and blurring roles and missions, the Army says the difference is that while the Space Force is focused on maintaining space superiority in orbit, its role is integrating space capability and effects into tactical multidomain operations from the ground.

Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an Oct. 13 interview that as demand for these capabilities grows, the Army needs to provide the same professional pathways and training for space operators that it does for other specializations, like artillery, infantry, and aviation.

“Training, education, experience, and talent management is how you create great leaders, and that’s how you build great units with great leaders,” Rafferty said. “It became apparent to the Army that in order to capitalize on the momentum, the gains that we’ve made in Army space-delivered capabilities, we need to professionalize the branch and do it fast.”
Rafferty highlighted a few areas where the Army expects to need more space personnel and effects in the coming years.

The service on Oct. 8 activated its a new Multi-Domain Task Force at Fort Carson, Colo., one of four elements stationed around the world and designed to integrate air, land, sea, space, and cyber operations in theater. A fifth is slated for activation in 2028. Each task force incorporates space effects, and Rafferty said that as the service adds more MDTFs, it will naturally need more space personnel and systems.

He also pointed to the creation of a new Theater Strike Effects Group at U.S. Army Pacific, which will require space support. The service also wants to expand the focus of its 1st Space Brigade—headquartered at Fort Carson, but distributed across six countries—beyond GPS, theater missile warning, and satellite communications into new capability areas. He did not provide details.

As for space systems, the Army hasn’t revealed plans to field its own satellites, but Rafferty and others said the service has an interest in building out an architecture of stratospheric platforms in the “near-space” region—between 60,000 and 100,000 feet in altitude.

“That’s a—no pun intended—space that is just ripe with potential, and the opportunities for various payloads to be on those is remarkable right now,” Rafferty said. “It’s affordable and scalable, and we’ve just got to really pursue that as part of the space branch growth.”

Mroszczyk described the region as a sort of transition point between the air and space domains where platforms could host a variety of payloads supporting missions like sensing and communications, and even serve as platforms for “launched effects”—the Army’s term for small, air- or ground-launched autonomous systems.

As an example, Mroszczyk said high-altitude platforms could form a “complementary” layer for some of the Space Force’s data transport efforts, like the Space Development Agency’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture or the Space Data Network. Systems in that layer could help distribute data during a conflict and provide resiliency should space systems be targeted.
He told reporters the Army is looking at a range of systems—from smaller platforms to larger balloons—and is planning multiple experiments in the coming year.

“That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from a stratospheric balloon,” he said.
SpaceX is preparing to launch a classified payload for the United States Space Force on Thursday afternoon from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

Liftoff of the Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 4 East is scheduled for 5:01 p.m. PDT (8:01 p.m. EDT / 0001 UTC). The mission, designated USSF-481, will take a southerly trajectory upon leaving the pad. Hazard warnings suggest that it will fly to a low Earth orbit inclined about 80 degrees from the Equator.

SpaceX will launch this mission using the Falcon 9 first stage booster B1081. This will be its 28th launch following four missions for NASA, three nationals security missions, two Transporter rideshare missions, two missions for Europe, and 16 Starlink missions.

A little more than eight minutes after liftoff, B1081 will target a landing on the droneship, Of Course I Still Love You, positioned in the Pacific Ocean. If successful, this will be the 228th landing on this vessel and the 671st Falcon booster landing to date.
The USSF-481 is also referenced as “TH-2” in public notices. It’s the second “TH” mission launched in as many months with the first being USSF-259 or TH-1 on Sept. 16.

Now on a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will soon reveal the universe’s darkest secrets. The mission launched at 7:26 a.m. EDT Sunday aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Roman pairs a large field of view with crisp infrared vision to explore vast swaths of the sky and probe deeply into cosmic history. This flagship mission will help astronomers explore dark matter, dark energy, and worlds outside of our solar system, known as exoplanets. Its surveys will support a broad range of research extending far beyond the mission’s main science goals.

The ground control team at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, began receiving telemetry data from Roman seven minutes after launch. The Falcon Heavy rocket performed as expected, separating from the observatory 31 minutes into the flight. After separating from the center core, the rocket’s boosters safely returned to the launch site for refurbishment.

The Roman team also confirmed successful deployment of the observatory’s solar panels and lower instrument sun shade an hour and 23 minutes after launch. Within the upcoming days, Roman’s high-gain antenna and visor-like deployable aperture cover will deploy, ground controllers will initiate the first of two-mid-course corrections, and the Coronagraph Instrument will power on. This instrument will demonstrate the technology that future missions like NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory concept could use to image Earth-like planets in the search for life in the universe. Roman’s Coronagraph will take a giant step in that direction by snapping pictures of Jupiter-like planets.

NASA is playing an important role in JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission, to advance our understanding of Mars’ moons and build on the agency’s long history of exploring the Red Planet.

The mission aims to characterize and determine the origin of Mars’ moons Phobos and Deimos and deliver a sample of Phobos to Earth. The MMX spacecraft is targeting launch from JAXA’s Tanegashima Space Center in Japan at 3:41 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 19 (4:41 a.m. JST on Tuesday, Oct. 20).

“The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “The NASA-JAXA sample curation partnership is extremely valuable, and I am proud that NASA Science is supporting MMX sample curation and will be sharing portions of these samples for study as we continue to expand humanity’s understanding of the universe for the benefit of all.”

NASA’s contributions to the mission include the Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE) spectrograph instrument, the Pneumatic Sampler (P-Sampler) technology demonstration, and communications and navigation support from the agency’s Deep Space Network, as well as funding United States scientists participating on the MMX science team.

Scientists have long debated the origin of Mars’ two moons. The data and samples collected by the MMX mission will help answer essential questions about the origins of these moons and the history of the solar system.

“Phobos and Deimos may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars’ gravity billions of years ago,” said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters. “Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds.”

The MEGANE (pronounced meh-GAH-nay, the Japanese word for eyeglasses) spectrograph will help scientists “see” what Phobos is made of by measuring neutrons and gamma rays emitted from the moon’s surface and determining its chemical elemental composition, which will provide important clues about its origin.

Mounted on one of the spacecraft’s landing legs, the P-Sampler is designed to collect a ground sample from Phobos. The system gathers surface material using bursts of high-pressure nitrogen gas, complementing JAXA’s C-Sampler, which will extract cores from a few inches deeper. NASA will obtain and curate about 15% of the total returned sample at the agency’s Johnson Space Center Astromaterials Lab in Houston, making it available for research for decades.

Another key part of NASA’s contribution to MMX is its scientific partnership with JAXA. NASA-supported researchers are working alongside international colleagues to help reveal the story of Phobos and will use mission data and returned samples to uncover new clues about the moon’s origin and the evolution of the Mars system.

The MMX spacecraft will arrive at Mars in August 2027 to begin its survey of the Red Planet’s two moons. After surveying Phobos in detail, the spacecraft will collect a sample of the moon’s surface no earlier than December 2028 and deliver it to Earth in 2031.

The MEGANE instrument was developed by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory. Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, developed the spacecraft’s pneumatic sampler mechanism. NASA’s contributions to the MMX mission were developed under the agency’s Discovery Program. The Discovery Program is managed by NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, for the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington.

People may think of soil as just dirt, but it is anything but inert. Beneath your feet, a vast network of mycorrhizal fungi is hard at work, trading minerals with plant roots. This trading system helps enrich the soil, and it sequesters 13 billion tons of atmospheric carbon dioxide each year — roughly equivalent to one-third of the world’s fossil-fuel emissions. Scientists know that these fungi form partnerships with 80% of all plant species on Earth, a relationship that evolved some 450 million years ago. What they have not understood is how organisms with no brain or central nervous system can decide whom to trade with, and on what terms.

Toby Kiers, an evolutionary biologist at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, has spent much of her career making this hidden world visible. Drawing on economics and game theory, and using tools that range from fluorescent quantum dots to imaging robots, her lab is probing how fungi and plants conduct their trade. The work raises new questions about soil, carbon, and even what counts as an individual organism. In this episode, Kiers tells co-host Steven Strogatz how these brainless, decentralized organisms can behave strategically — discriminating between better and worse partners and shifting resources across the network to wherever a plant will “pay” more for it — and how she has built a worldwide community of researchers to map the biodiversity of these underground networks and advocate for their protection.

Scientists have uncovered a promising new way to protect some of the world's most important food crops from a destructive fungus that threatens global food security. By engineering the natural immune defenses of plants, researchers have developed an experimental approach that could eventually help wheat, rice, and barley resist fungal infections more effectively.

The international research team, led by scientists at the John Innes Centre in the United Kingdom, investigated a recently discovered group of plant immune receptors. They identified how these proteins recognize invading pathogens and demonstrated that they can be modified to detect multiple fungal threats. The findings could open the door to crops with stronger, more durable disease resistance.

"We've discovered something that could lead to a potential intervention on what is the worst fungal disease of cereals," said Professor Mark Banfield, a research group leader at the John Innes Centre and an author of the study, which involved collaborators at Kobe University in Japan.
A Devastating Fungus Threatens the Global Food Supply

The target of the research is Magnaporthe oryzae, the fungus responsible for blast disease. It causes the most serious fungal disease affecting cultivated rice and has also become a major threat to wheat and barley in parts of Asia and Africa.

The damage is enormous. Each year, rice blast destroys enough rice to feed approximately 60 million people. As the fungus spreads into additional agricultural regions, developing effective ways to protect crops has become increasingly important for global food security.

The fungus infects plants through a sophisticated biological strategy. It delivers specialized molecules known as effectors into cells in the leaves and stems. These molecules interfere with normal plant functions, allowing the pathogen to establish an infection and promote disease.

Plants, however, have evolved their own defense systems. Specialized immune receptors can recognize these foreign molecules and trigger a protective response. One important mechanism involves causing infected cells to die in a controlled, localized area, helping prevent the pathogen from spreading farther through the plant.
Scientists Discover a Hidden Plant Immune Defense

For more than three decades, much of the research into plant immunity has centered on proteins called Nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich receptors (NLRs). These receptors have played a central role in understanding how crops recognize and defend themselves against blast disease and other infections.

More recently, scientists have begun investigating another group of immune proteins found in cereal crops, known as tandem kinase proteins (TKPs). Although researchers are still learning how these receptors operate, they appear to offer additional opportunities for strengthening plant defenses.

Earlier studies revealed that some TKPs contain a specialized region called a Heavy Metal Associated (HMA) domain. Similar regions are also found in certain NLR receptors, where they help recognize pathogen effectors and initiate immune responses.
This shared feature attracted the attention of Banfield and his colleagues because it suggested that scientists might be able to redesign the receptors to recognize additional fungal threats.

"This piqued our interest," said Professor Banfield. "If we can engineer these integrated HMA domains for new properties by making amino acid protein changes where effectors bind, we can gain what we call novel recognition specificities - and potentially a new frontline for defense of plants against disease."
Turning Fungal Attack Molecules Into Targets
In the study, published in Science Advances, researchers examined precisely how HMA domains interact with the molecules released by the blast fungus.

Using biophysical techniques and crystallography, a method that allows scientists to determine the detailed three-dimensional structure of molecules, the team obtained a high-resolution view of how these plant receptors bind to fungal effectors.

The results revealed that HMA domains can function as biological bait. By binding to molecules the fungus uses during infection, these regions help plants recognize the presence of an invading pathogen and activate their defenses.
Armed with this structural information, the researchers modified TKP immune receptors so they could recognize two different fungal effectors associated with infections in wheat and barley.

This ability to detect multiple targets, known as dual specificity, is unusual in naturally occurring immune receptors. Demonstrating that it can be introduced through protein engineering suggests a promising way to expand the range of threats that crop immune systems can recognize.

The findings also provide a foundation for investigating other recently identified TKPs in different cereal crops. Scientists may eventually be able to design customized immune receptors that detect several fungal effectors simultaneously, potentially making plants more difficult for pathogens to infect.
Engineering Crops With Stronger Disease Resistance
Although the findings are encouraging, the technology remains at an early experimental stage.

The researchers conducted their initial tests using protoplasts, individual wheat cells that serve as a simplified model for studying how plant tissues respond. The next step is to determine whether the engineered receptors can provide effective protection in whole plants grown under controlled greenhouse conditions.

"Our study indicates that this new class of resistance proteins is amenable for engineering purposes. We now know that the previous tools we used in engineering NLR receptors may also work with this new class," said Dr. Daniel Yu, the first author of the study.

Understanding exactly how fungal effectors attach to plant immune receptors could also help researchers take advantage of other technologies. Precision breeding and artificial intelligence may provide additional ways to redesign HMA domains, allowing them to recognize pathogen molecules that previously escaped detection.
One particularly promising possibility involves combining different types of immune receptors within the same crop.

Because NLRs and TKPs appear to activate plant defenses through different mechanisms, using them together could create several layers of protection. This might make it harder for fungi to evolve ways around a plant's immune system.

"We think these two classes of immune receptors, NLRs and TKPs, are probably activated in different ways," said Professor Banfield. "That gives the potential for more robust immunity in the field because you are not putting all your eggs in one basket. Further down the road, we may be able to use techniques to stack genes encoding TKPs and NLRs together against the same disease, making a super-resistant crop. They will have different ways of activating immunity, so it is likely to be more difficult for a pathogen to evolve away from," he added.
A Growing Threat to Wheat, Rice, and Barley
The need for better protection is becoming more urgent as blast disease continues to threaten major food crops.

Wheat blast was first identified in Brazil during the 1980s and has since spread to parts of Asia and Africa. Although the disease has not been detected in the United Kingdom, climate change could eventually create conditions that allow it to threaten cereal production in northern Europe.
For farmers, the emergence of blast disease in new regions presents a serious challenge, particularly because the fungus can threaten crops that are essential to feeding large populations.

By revealing how a previously underexplored class of plant immune receptors can be engineered to recognize multiple fungal threats, the researchers have identified a possible new strategy for protecting future harvests.

Further testing will be necessary to establish whether these modified defenses work effectively in whole plants and under agricultural conditions. If successful, combining different immune receptors could eventually help scientists develop crops with more resilient protection against one of agriculture's most destructive fungal diseases.
